content: Normocytic anemia is a prevalent condition, particularly among individuals aged 85 years and older. Its occurrence becomes more frequent with advancing age, affecting up to 44 percent of men over the age of 85. This type of anemia is the most commonly observed form of anemia. Normocytic anemia can result from several underlying mechanisms. These include a reduced production of red blood cells that are normal in size, as seen in conditions such as anemia of chronic disease or aplastic anemia. It may also arise from an increased destruction or loss of red blood cells, which occurs in cases of hemolysis or post-hemorrhagic anemia. Additionally, an uncompensated expansion of plasma volume, such as that seen during pregnancy or in states of fluid overload, can contribute to the development of normocytic anemia. In some cases, it may result from a combination of factors that simultaneously produce both microcytic and macrocytic anemia. For a thorough evaluation of anemia and its differential diagnosis, further resources or diagnostic tools should be consulted.
